nt: Here, **to the face of** represents being in front of the altar. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [before the altar of]

x.ASV: And thou shalt answer and say before Jehovah thy God, A Syrian ready to perish was my father; and he went down into Egypt, and sojourned there, few in number; and he became there a nation, great, mighty, and populous.
x.Darby: And thou shalt speak and say before Jehovah thyGod, A perishing Aramaean was my father, and he went down to Egypt with a few, and sojourned there, and became there a nation, great, mighty, and populous.
x.KJV: And thou shalt speak and say before the Lord thy God, A Syrian ready to perish was my father, and he went down into Egypt, and sojourned there with a few, and became there a nation, great, mighty, and populous:
x.YLT: `And thou hast answered and said before Jehovah thy God, A perishing Aramaean is my father! and he goeth down to Egypt, and sojourneth there with few men, and becometh there a nation, great, mighty, and numerous;

nt: Moses is instructing the people to **respond** with the following statement as part of this ceremony, rather than to answer what someone said to them. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [After the priest does that, say]

The phrase **and say** introduces a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. It may not be necessary to represent both verbs explicitly. Alternate translation: [And you shall say]

Here, **to the face of** represents being in front of or in the presence of Yahweh. See the Introduction to Deuteronomy for a discussion of this phrase. See how you translated it in [1:45](../01/45.md). Alternate translation: [in the presence of Yahweh your God] or [before Yahweh your God]

The speaker assumes that readers will know that he is referring to his ancestor, Jacob, who lived for many years in Aram Naharaim before settling in Egypt. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [My ancestor was Jacob, who lived as a foreigner in Aram] or [My ancestor was Jacob, who wandered in the land of Aram]

In keeping with what is usual for his language and culture, the speaker is marking travel for change in elevation. If this expression contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [And he went]

Here, **he** represents Jacob’s descendants. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and there Jacob’s descendants became] or [and there the Israelites became]

The terms **great** and **mighty** mean similar things. Moses is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [a very powerful]

x.ASV: And the Egyptians dealt ill with us, and afflicted us, and laid upon us hard bondage:
x.Darby: And the Egyptians evil-entreated us, and afflicted us, and laid upon us hard bondage;
x.KJV: And the Egyptians evil entreated us, and afflicted us, and laid upon us hard bondage:
x.YLT: and the Egyptians do us evil, and afflict us, and put on us hard service;

nt: The terms **treated us badly** and **afflicted us** mean similar things. The speaker is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [And the Egyptians mistreated us severely]
By **us**, the speaker means to include both himself and his listeners, so use the inclusive form of that word if your language marks that distinction.

Here the speaker is speaking of the hard labor that the Egyptians required the Israelites to do as if it were an object that they could **set upon** them. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And they forced us to do hard labor] or [And they oppressed us with hard labor]

x.ASV: and we cried unto Jehovah, the God of our fathers, and Jehovah heard our voice, and saw our affliction, and our toil, and our oppression;
x.Darby: and we cried to Jehovah, theGod of our fathers, and Jehovah heard our voice, and looked on our affliction, and our labour, and our oppression;

x.YLT: and we cry unto Jehovah, God of our fathers, and Jehovah heareth our voice, and seeth our affliction, and our labour, and our oppression;

nt: The Israelites are using **cried out** as a common expression of their culture to mean “we prayed urgently for help.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And we prayed desperately to Yahweh] or [And we called to Yahweh for help]

The speaker is using **heard our voice** as a common expression of his culture to mean “heard us when we prayed” or “responded to our prayer.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and Yahweh answered our prayer]

Here, **voice** represents what the Israelites said when they prayed. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [our prayer] or [our cry for help]

The terms **affliction** and **labor** and **oppression** are abstract nouns. If your language does not use abstract nouns for these ideas, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [how badly they treated us and how hard they made us work and how they oppressed us]

x.ASV: and Jehovah brought us forth out of Egypt with a mighty hand, and with an outstretched arm, and with great terribleness, and with signs, and with wonders;
x.Darby: and Jehovah brought us forth out of Egypt with a powerful hand, and with a stretched-out arm, and with great terribleness, and with signs, and with wonders;
x.KJV: And the Lord brought us forth out of Egypt with a mighty hand, and with an outstretched arm, and with great terribleness, and with signs, and with wonders:

nt: See how you translated the similar phrase “by a mighty hand and by an outstretched arm” in [4:34](../04/34.md). Alternate translation: [by showing his mighty power]

Here the expressions **mighty hand** and **outstretched arm** represent Yahweh’s great power. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [with his overwhelming power] or [by showing his mighty power]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **fearsomeness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [in a way that caused people to be very afraid]

x.ASV: and he hath brought us into this place, and hath given us this land, a land flowing with milk and honey.
x.Darby: and he hath brought us into this place, and hath given us this land, a land flowing with milk and honey!
x.KJV: And he hath brought us into this place, and hath given us this land, even a land that floweth with milk and honey.

nt: See how you translated the phrase “a land flowing with milk and honey” in [6:3](../06/03.md).

לִ⁠פְנֵי֙ יְהוָ֣ה אֱלֹהֶ֔י⁠ךָ וְ⁠הִֽשְׁתַּחֲוִ֔יתָ לִ⁠פְנֵ֖י יְהוָ֥ה אֱלֹהֶֽי⁠ךָ

Here, **to the face of** represents being in front of or in the presence of Yahweh. See the Introduction to Deuteronomy for a discussion of this phrase. See how you translated it in [1:45](../01/45.md). Alternate translation: [in the presence of Yahweh your God and bow down before Yahweh your God]

x.ASV: and thou shalt rejoice in all the good which Jehovah thy God hath given unto thee, and unto thy house, thou, and the Levite, and the sojourner that is in the midst of thee.

nt: Here, **your house** represents an entire household living together. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and to your household]

Here, **the Levite** and **the foreigner** represent Levites and foreigners in general, not specific individuals. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use expressions that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and any Levites and foreigners who are among you] or [and all the Levites and foreigners who are among you]

x.ASV: When thou hast made an end of tithing all the tithe of thine increase in the third year, which is the year of tithing, then thou shalt give it unto the Levite, to the sojourner, to the fatherless, and to the widow, that they may eat within thy gates, and be filled.
x.Darby: When thou hast made an end of tithing all the tithes of thy produce in the third year, the year of tithing, thou shalt give it to the Levite, to the stranger, to the fatherless, and to the widow, that they may eat in thy gates, and be filled;
x.KJV: When thou hast made an end of tithing all the tithes of thine increase the third year, which is the year of tithing, and hast given it unto the Levite, the stranger, the fatherless, and the widow, that they may eat within thy gates, and be filled;
x.YLT: `When thou dost complete to tithe all the tithe of thine increase in the third year, the year of the tithe, then thou hast given to the Levite, to the sojourner, to the fatherless, and to the widow, and they have eaten within thy gates, and been satisfied,

nt: Moses is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [gathering all the tithes of] or [the collection of all your offerings of]
If your language would not represent a number in a form such as **in the third year**, you could represent this number in a form that your language would use. Alternate translation: [in year three]

The **year of tithing** refers to a special offering collected every three years that the Israelites give as an additional tithe for the poor. See this instruction in [14:28](../14/28.md). If your readers would not be familiar with what a year of tithing is, you could use a more general term or explain it in a footnote. Alternate translation: [in the third year, when a special tithe was collected for the poor]

Moses is not referring to specific **Levites**, **foreigners**, **fatherless**, or **widows**. He means these groups of people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use expressions that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [to all the Levites, foreigners, orphans, and widows]
See how you translated the phrase “within your gates” in [5:14](../05/14.md). Alternate translation: [in any of your communities] or [among your people]

x.ASV: And thou shalt say before Jehovah thy God, I have put away the hallowed things out of my house, and also have given them unto the Levite, and unto the sojourner, to the fatherless, and to the widow, according to all thy commandment which thou hast commanded me: I have not transgressed any of thy commandments, neither have I forgotten them:

nt: The word translated as **the things set apart** is referring to those things that were considered sacred or dedicated to God. Here it refers to a kind of offering, the tithe, that people dedicated to God from their harvest. If your readers would not be familiar with this phrase, you could use a more general term or explain it in a footnote. Alternate translation: [the sacred tenth portion] or [the holy tithe]

Here, **to the face of** represents being in front of or in the presence of Yahweh. See the Introduction to Deuteronomy for a discussion of this phrase. See how you translated it in [1:45](../01/45.md). Alternate translation: [in the presence of] or [before]

The speaker is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [I have not transgressed any of your commandments, neither have I forgotten your commandments]

x.ASV: I have not eaten thereof in my mourning, neither have I put away thereof, being unclean, nor given thereof for the dead: I have hearkened to the voice of Jehovah my God; I have done according to all that thou hast commanded me.
x.Darby: I have not eaten thereof in my mourning, neither have I brought away thereof in uncleanness, nor given thereof for a dead person; I have hearkened to the voice of Jehovah myGod; I have done according to all that thou hast commanded me.
x.KJV: I have not eaten thereof in my mourning, neither have I taken away ought thereof for any unclean use, nor given ought thereof for the dead: but I have hearkened to the voice of the Lord my God, and have done according to all that thou hast commanded me.
x.YLT: I have not eaten in mine affliction of it, nor have I put away of it for uncleanness, nor have I given of it for the dead; I have hearkened to the voice of Jehovah my God; I have done according to all that Thou hast commanded me;

nt: A **mourning** here refers to a state of ritual uncleanness that occurred when someone had contact with a dead body. During this time, a person was not allowed to handle holy things. If your readers would not be familiar with this concept, you could use a more general term or explain it in a footnote. Alternate translation: [while I was ritually unclean] or [during a time when I was ceremonially impure]

The phrase **in sin** refers to any condition that would have made a person ritually unclean or unacceptable to God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express this meaning more clearly. Alternate translation: [while I was ritually unclean]

The phrase **given from it to the dead** refers to making offerings to the spirits of dead people. This was a pagan religious practice that was forbidden in Israel. If your readers would not be familiar with this practice, you could use a more general term or explain it in a footnote. Alternate translation: [have I offered any of it in worship of the dead] or [have I used any of it as offerings to dead people]

Moses assumes that readers will know that **listen** as it is used here, includes the meaning of “obey.” You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. The phrases **walk in his ways** and **keep his statutes and his commandments and his ordinances** and **listen to his voice** mean basically the same thing. The second and third phrases emphasize the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and it would be good to show this to your readers by including all three phrases in your translation, if possible. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second and third phrases are repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [follow his ways by obeying all his commands and doing everything he tells you]

Here Moses is speaking of the **commandments** of Yahweh as if they were **ways** or a path that the people should **walk** on. He means that obeying those commandments is like walking on that path. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and you shall live as he wants you to] or [and you shall obey his instructions]
See how you translated the terms “statutes,” “commandments,” and “ordinances” in [5:31](../05/31.md).
See how you translated the phrase “listen to his voice” in [4:30](../04/30.md).
